summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Mozambique. The 2015 revision of the penal code struck the colonial-era "vices against nature" provision, and the code now in force, Law 24/2019 (effective 2020), carries no prohibition on consensual conduct and no provision criminalising gender identity. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on that basis.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists in Mozambican law. Outright International's country entry, updated March 2026, records the continued absence of any mechanism for a person to change legal gender markers. A 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of Mozambicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender; that measures public opinion rather than an available procedure, and its fieldwork closed in 2017.

The penal code addresses anti-trans conduct through incitement and sentencing provisions. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on the basis of gender identity, and reaches defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 treats a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating factor in homicide. No prosecution brought under either article is recorded in this inventory.

No statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024, and Outright International's March 2026 entry records the same removal of employment non-discrimination protection. The Advertising Code of 2016 bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on sexual-orientation grounds; the source text does not extend that code to gender identity.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt, and protests demanding same-sex marriage and common-law recognition have run since 2006.

Organised protection machinery exists and was established through the courts. Lambda Mozambique's NGO registration was blocked from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council ruled that Lambda's status did not violate the constitution and struck down the "moral order" clause of Article 1 of Law No. 8/91 that had been used to refuse registration, unblocking the country's only LGBT organisation (Global Voices, 28 November 2017).

Outright International's March 2026 entry describes societal attitudes as broadly neutral while recording family ostracisation and barriers to employment and education for LGBTIQ people. The 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations and then disappointed them. Lambda's Carina Capitine told the Guardian in June 2015 that the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination; no later dated assessment of violence appears in this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
Attitude survey evidence is dated and measures views of gay, lesbian and bisexual people rather than trans-specific risk. A 2017 survey found support for same-sex marriage at 47% in Maputo, 38% in Beira and 42% in Nampula, and found most respondents would not accept a child who came out, with 28% of Beira respondents stating they would assault their child if he or she was gay; in the same survey 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and said they would help if someone were being physically assaulted, and about one-third of respondents personally knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2017 ILGA poll found 61% of Mozambicans agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as heterosexual people. A 2013 survey found moderate support for parenting rights.

Afrobarometer data reported by Erasing 76 Crimes in March 2016 placed Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant countries, with 56% saying they would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, against 5% in Uganda, Burkina Faso and Niger. The comparison is between countries on an attitude measure, not a measure of violence or legal exposure.

The Human Rights Watch World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests. It contains no transgender-specific content and no information on where trans prisoners are housed.

The GlobalGayz archive covers 2006 to 2011 and documents early organising under the colonial-era law: the first newspaper article arguing gay rights appeared in Agencia de Informacao on 7 July 2006, Maputo men petitioned parliament, the LGBT group was still unregistered as of March 2011, and the archive records refugee deaths en route to South Africa. These are dated milestones, not current conditions.

The employment non-discrimination protection that had been in place since 2007 was repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024, so a Mozambican dismissed on these grounds has no statutory claim under that provision.

Outright International's March 2026 entry records family ostracisation and barriers to employment and education as the lived position of LGBTIQ Mozambicans, alongside broadly neutral societal attitudes. The 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised expectations within the community that were then disappointed.

Lambda Mozambique operates as the country's only LGBT organisation after a decade of blocked registration applications beginning in 2008, a UN appeal in 2010, and the October 2017 Constitutional Council ruling that struck the "moral order" clause used to refuse it status. Its lobbying pivoted to anti-discrimination work after the 2015 penal code removed the colonial provision.

Residents cannot change legal gender markers, cannot enter a recognised relationship with a partner of the same gender, and cannot marry or adopt as a same-sex couple. Public opinion recorded in 2017 was divided on relationship recognition and, in the same year, 55% of respondents in an ILGA poll supported allowing transgender people to change their legal gender.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence figure, killing count or rate appears in this inventory for Mozambique, and none is carried here. The only dated violence assessment is Lambda's Carina Capitine statement to the Guardian of 30 June 2015 that the community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries; no later dated assessment is sourced.

Whether Articles 191 and 160 of Law 24/2019 have been applied in any prosecution is unresolved: the inventory supplies the statutory text but no case records.

The inventory does not state whether the Advertising Code of 2016 extends beyond sexual orientation to gender identity; only sexual-orientation grounds are given in the source text.

The instrument that removed employment non-discrimination protection is described inconsistently across sources: one entry attributes it to Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024, and another refers to a 2024 penal-code change without identifying a provision. This is unresolved in the sources.

No information is sourced on where trans prisoners would be housed in Mozambique, on入境 screening or document-marker treatment of trans travellers, or on access to gender-affirming care. The Human Rights Watch World Report 2024 chapter for Mozambique addresses none of these.

All survey figures cited here have fieldwork windows that closed in 2013 or 2017; no more recent public-opinion data on gender identity or sexual orientation is present in the inventory.
